title: Rotate Image (in-place 90°)
description: Rotate an n×n matrix 90° clockwise in place by transposing then reversing each row.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given an n×n matrix and I need to rotate it 90° clockwise — and the catch is it has to be in place, no allocating a second matrix."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Always square (n×n), or can it be rectangular? (90° rotation of a rectangle would change the shape, so square is the norm.)
• Clockwise specifically, or should I handle counter-clockwise too?
• In place means O(1) extra space — no second matrix — right?
• Return value — mutate and return nothing, or return the same reference?
sections.why: The in-place constraint is the whole point of the problem — the obvious O(n²)-space solution (allocate a new matrix, write `out[j][n-1-i] = matrix[i][j]`) is trivial. Confirming square is also load-bearing: a rectangular rotation can't be done in place because the dimensions swap. Asking these up front signals you noticed the constraint isn't decorative — it's what makes the problem worth asking.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n²)-space solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is straightforward: allocate a new n×n matrix `out`, then for every (i, j) in the input, write `out[j][n-1-i] = matrix[i][j]`. That's the direct rotation formula — a cell at (i, j) lands at (j, n-1-i) after a 90° CW turn. O(n²) time, O(n²) space. Then copy `out` back over `matrix` cell by cell if I have to mutate in place. Works, but it fails the 'no extra matrix' constraint, and the copy-back step is wasteful."
sections.why: Two reasons to name it. (1) It surfaces the rotation formula `(i, j) → (j, n-1-i)` — that formula is exactly the math identity we're about to factor into two simpler operations. (2) It frames the optimization: we're not inventing a new algorithm, we're factoring the same map into two passes that each happen to be in-place-friendly (a swap-based transpose, a row reverse).

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What's the math identity that makes the two-pass trick work?
sections.say:
"The trick is recognizing that 90° CW rotation equals transpose then row-reverse. Let me verify the math:
• Transpose: (i, j) → (j, i).
• Then reverse row j: (j, i) → (j, n-1-i).
• Compose: (i, j) → (j, n-1-i). ✓ — exactly the rotation formula.

Both operations are in-place: transpose swaps pairs across the main diagonal (no allocation), row-reverse is `Array.prototype.reverse()` per row (in-place). So composing two in-place ops gives an in-place rotation. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space."
sections.why: Naming the pattern *and* deriving the math is the move. 'Transpose then reverse rows' alone is a memorized recipe; verifying `(i, j) → (j, i) → (j, n-1-i)` lands at the rotation formula is the derivation. Interviewers grade on the second — and it lets you generate the counter-clockwise variant on the spot (reverse rows first, *then* transpose — or transpose then reverse columns) without re-memorizing a separate trick.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the two-pass model before writing the loops.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the standard 3×3, the tiniest non-trivial case (2×2), and a 4×4 where the two phases are easier to eyeball separately.

examples.note: Classic 3×3 — the diagonal (1, 5, 9) stays fixed across the transpose; row reverse then flips horizontally.
examples.trace:
input:        transpose:    reverse rows:
[1, 2, 3]     [1, 4, 7]     [7, 4, 1]
[4, 5, 6]     [2, 5, 8]     [8, 5, 2]
[7, 8, 9]     [3, 6, 9]     [9, 6, 3]

transpose swaps (i, j) with (j, i) for j > i:
  swap (0, 1)↔(1, 0): 2 ↔ 4
  swap (0, 2)↔(2, 0): 3 ↔ 7
  swap (1, 2)↔(2, 1): 6 ↔ 8
then reverse each row in place.

examples.note: Smallest non-trivial — only one transpose swap (2 ↔ 3) and two row reverses. Easy to verify by hand.
examples.trace:
input:        transpose:    reverse rows:
[1, 2]        [1, 3]        [3, 1]
[3, 4]        [2, 4]        [4, 2]

transpose: swap (0, 1)↔(1, 0): 2 ↔ 3
reverse row 0: [1, 3] → [3, 1]
reverse row 1: [2, 4] → [4, 2]

examples.note: 4×4 makes the off-by-one in the transpose loop visible — j starts at i+1 so the swap (1, 2)↔(2, 1) happens, but (2, 1)↔(1, 2) doesn't repeat. If you set j=0, every pair swaps twice and you're back to the original.

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the killer off-by-one — the inner loop must start at `j = i + 1`, not `j = 0`. If you set `j = 0`, every pair (i, j) and (j, i) swaps twice, which restores the original matrix. The 4×4 trace makes the pair count explicit (6 swaps = n(n-1)/2), which is the right way to defend the 'starting at i+1' choice to a skeptical interviewer.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• n = 0 (empty matrix) → loops don't execute, nothing to do. ✓
• n = 1 (single cell) → transpose loop body never runs (j starts at i+1 = 1, never < 1), reverse on a 1-element row is a no-op. ✓
• n = 2 → one transpose swap, two row reverses — smallest case that actually does work.
• Rectangular m × n where m ≠ n — the in-place trick doesn't apply; the shape changes after rotation. Worth flagging that the algorithm assumes square; if rectangular is in scope, I'd allocate `out` of size n × m.
• Counter-clockwise variant — reverse rows first then transpose, or transpose then reverse columns. Same math identity, different composition order.
• 180° rotation — apply this algorithm twice, or simpler: reverse all rows AND reverse the row order."
sections.why: Edge-case enumeration is the difference between 'works on the example' and 'production-ready'. The rectangular call-out in particular shows depth — most candidates assume square without noticing they assumed it. The 180°/counter-clockwise extensions show that you see the algorithm as a composition of primitive operations (transpose, reverse rows, reverse columns), not as a frozen recipe.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n²) — transpose does n(n-1)/2 swaps (so n²/2 - n/2), and the row reverses do n*n/2 element swaps total. Both are Θ(n²), so the whole thing is O(n²). You can't do better than O(n²) because every one of the n² cells has to move.

Space is O(1) extra — the swaps and reverses are all in-place. No auxiliary matrix.

The 'compose two simpler in-place operations' template extends to other matrix problems: 180° = reverse rows + reverse column order (or apply 90° twice); 90° counter-clockwise = transpose + reverse columns (or reverse rows + transpose). Reflect across the anti-diagonal? That's `(i, j) → (n-1-j, n-1-i)` — transpose + reverse both rows and columns. Once you see rotations and reflections as compositions of transpose and reverse, the whole family becomes one template."
sections.why: The O(n²) lower bound argument ('every cell must move') is what wins the pushback 'can you do better?'. The composition-template framing — naming counter-clockwise, 180°, and anti-diagonal reflection as variations of the same primitives — proves you see the family, not just this one problem. That's how the same shape powers any 'rotate/reflect an in-place grid' question.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the two-phase rotation: transpose across the main diagonal, then reverse each row. The state panel snapshots the matrix after each swap so you can see the reflection forming, then watch the rows flip.
trace: function* trace(input) {
const matrix = input.matrix;
const snap = () => matrix.map(row => row.slice());
yield { line: 1, label: `enter function — matrix is ${matrix.length}x${matrix.length}`, state: { matrix: snap() } };
const n = matrix.length;
yield { line: 2, label: `n = ${n}`, state: { matrix: snap(), n } };
yield { line: 3, label: 'PHASE 1: transpose (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i)', state: { matrix: snap(), n } };
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
yield { line: 4, label: `outer transpose: i=${i}`, state: { matrix: snap(), n, i } };
for (let j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
yield { line: 5, label: `inner: j=${j} — about to swap matrix[${i}][${j}](${matrix[i][j]}) with matrix[${j}][${i}](${matrix[j][i]})`, state: { matrix: snap(), n, i, j } };
const tmp = matrix[i][j];
matrix[i][j] = matrix[j][i];
matrix[j][i] = tmp;
yield { line: 6, label: `swapped — matrix[${i}][${j}]=${matrix[i][j]}, matrix[${j}][${i}]=${matrix[j][i]}`, state: { matrix: snap(), n, i, j } };
yield { line: 8, label: 'transpose complete — matrix reflected across main diagonal', state: { matrix: snap(), n } };
yield { line: 9, label: 'PHASE 2: reverse each row in place → completes 90° CW rotation', state: { matrix: snap(), n } };
for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
const before = matrix[i].slice();
matrix[i].reverse();
yield { line: 10, label: `row ${i}: [${before.join(',')}] → [${matrix[i].join(',')}]`, state: { matrix: snap(), n, i } };
yield { line: 10, label: `done — final matrix = ${JSON.stringify(matrix)}`, state: { matrix: snap(), n, returns: JSON.stringify(matrix) } };

reference.approach: Transpose across the main diagonal, then reverse each row
notes: Transpose + row-reverse equals 90° clockwise. Reverse columns instead for counter-clockwise.
Inner loop starts at `j = i + 1` so you don't swap each pair twice (and back to original).
In-place — no auxiliary matrix. Mutating the input is the whole point of the problem.

alternates.label: New-matrix (direct formula)
alternates.when: Use when in-place is not required and clarity matters more than space — the direct formula `out[j][n-1-i] = matrix[i][j]` is immediately readable and easy to verify. Fails the in-place constraint of the standard interview problem.
notes: Direct rotation formula: cell (i, j) lands at (j, n-1-i) after 90° CW.
Allocates an n×n auxiliary matrix — O(n²) extra space, which violates the typical in-place constraint.
Use the transpose+reverse two-pass variant whenever in-place is required.

questions.q: Which two operations compose into a 90° clockwise rotation?
questions.explain: Transposing reflects across the main diagonal; reversing each row then flips horizontally, equivalent to a 90° clockwise rotation.

questions.q: Why does the transpose loop start `j` at `i + 1`?
options: To skip the diagonal — the diagonal cells need a separate self-swap, handled outside the loop
To avoid swapping each pair twice (which restores the original)
Because `j = i` would make the row-reverse phase double-flip the diagonal cells, undoing them
Because `matrix[i][i]` is read-only by convention in in-place rotations to preserve the trace
questions.explain: With `j = 0` the loop visits both `(i,j)` and `(j,i)`, swapping each pair a second time and restoring the original matrix exactly. The diagonal needs no special handling — `matrix[i][i]` would just swap with itself.

options: O(n^2) time, O(n) extra space for the per-row reverse buffers
questions.explain: The transpose touches each of the ~n²/2 off-diagonal pairs once and the row reverses add another ~n²/2 swaps. Everything mutates `matrix` directly; `Array.prototype.reverse` is in-place too (it is `toReversed` that allocates), so only a temp swap variable is ever held.

questions.q: To rotate 90° counter-clockwise with the same trick, what changes?
options: Apply the 90° CW algorithm three times — three CW rotations equal one CCW
Transpose, then reverse each column (or reverse rows first, then transpose)
Reverse the whole matrix once (treating it as a flat array of n^2 cells)
Transpose across the ANTI-diagonal instead of the main diagonal, then reverse rows
questions.explain: Transpose is its own reflection — the second flip picks the direction. Reversing each ROW after the transpose gives clockwise; reversing each COLUMN (equivalently, reversing each row BEFORE transposing) gives counter-clockwise: `[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]` becomes `[[3,6,9],[2,5,8],[1,4,7]]`.

L3.prompt: Write `rotate(matrix)` that rotates an n×n matrix 90° clockwise in place. Log `JSON.stringify(matrix)` after rotating [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]].
hints: Transpose first: swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i.
Then reverse each row in place.
